claim: The General Stress Response promotes survival of bacteria in adverse conditions.
source: The General Stress Response promotes survival of bacteria in adverse conditions, but how sensor proteins transduce species-specific signals to initiate the response is not known.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about bacterial stress responses.

claim: The mechanism by which sensor proteins transduce species-specific signals to initiate the General Stress Response is not known.
source: The General Stress Response promotes survival of bacteria in adverse conditions, but how sensor proteins transduce species-specific signals to initiate the response is not known.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The serine/threonine phosphatase RsbU initiates the General Stress Response in Bacillus subtilis upon binding a partner protein (RsbT).
source: The serine/threonine phosphatase RsbU initiates the General Stress Response in Bacillus subtilis upon binding a partner protein (RsbT) that is released from sequestration by environmental stresses.
evidence: This is supported by prior research and is a foundational statement for the study.

claim: RsbT is released from sequestration by environmental stresses.
source: The serine/threonine phosphatase RsbU initiates the General Stress Response in Bacillus subtilis upon binding a partner protein (RsbT) that is released from sequestration by environmental stresses.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about the stressosome mechanism.

claim: RsbT activates RsbU by inducing otherwise flexible linkers of RsbU to form a short coiled-coil.
source: We report that RsbT activates RsbU by inducing otherwise flexible linkers of RsbU to form a short coiled-coil that dimerizes and activates the phosphatase domains.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by SAXS data and biochemical assays.

claim: The coiled-coil formed by RsbU linkers dimerizes and activates the phosphatase domains.
source: We report that RsbT activates RsbU by inducing otherwise flexible linkers of RsbU to form a short coiled-coil that dimerizes and activates the phosphatase domains.
evidence: This is supported by structural predictions and biochemical data showing increased phosphatase activity.

claim: Related coiled-coil linkers and phosphatase dimers transduce signals from diverse sensor domains to control the General Stress Response across bacterial phyla.
source: Importantly, we present evidence that related coiled-coil linkers and phosphatase dimers transduce signals from diverse sensor domains to control the General Stress Response and other signaling across bacterial phyla.
evidence: This is supported by AlphaFold2 predictions of multiple phosphatases from different bacterial species.

claim: The coiled-coil linker transduction mechanism provides a resolution to how shared sensory domains control serine/threonine phosphatases, diguanylate cyclases and histidine kinases.
source: This coiled-coil linker transduction mechanism additionally suggests a resolution to the mystery of how shared sensory domains control serine/threonine phosphatases, diguanylate cyclases and histidine kinases.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural similarities observed in AlphaFold2 predictions.

claim: The coiled-coil linker mechanism provides bacteria with a modularly exchangeable toolkit for the evolution of diverse signaling pathways.
source: We propose that this provides bacteria with a modularly exchangeable toolkit for the evolution of diverse signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed conservation of the mechanism.

claim: The General Stress Response controls transcription of a large and diverse set of genes.
source: A defining feature of the GSR is that it controls transcription of a large and diverse set of genes, dramatically reshaping the physiology of the organism (Gottesman, 2019; Guerreiro et al., 2020; Boekhoud et al., 2020; Boylan et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The General Stress Response dramatically reshapes the physiology of the organism.
source: A defining feature of the GSR is that it controls transcription of a large and diverse set of genes, dramatically reshaping the physiology of the organism (Gottesman, 2019; Guerreiro et al., 2020; Boekhoud et al., 2020; Boylan et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The GSR is induced by a variety of stress conditions including stationary phase, nutrient depletion, cellular damage, and host defense mechanisms.
source: Another defining feature is that the GSR is induced by a variety of stress conditions that are frequently associated with each other, including stationary phase, nutrient depletion, cellular damage, and (for pathogens) host defense mechanisms (Gottesman, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The multiplicity of initiating conditions allows cells to anticipate and prepare for accumulating adversity.
source: This multiplicity of initiating conditions allows cells to anticipate and prepare for accumulating adversity, suggesting why the GSR is present in every bacterial species that has so far been analyzed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed characteristics of the GSR.

claim: The GSR is present in every bacterial species that has so far been analyzed.
source: This multiplicity of initiating conditions allows cells to anticipate and prepare for accumulating adversity, suggesting why the GSR is present in every bacterial species that has so far been analyzed.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The GSR contributes to pathogenesis through expression of genes controlling virulence, biofilm formation, and quorum sensing.
source: The GSR additionally contributes to pathogenesis through expression of genes controlling virulence, biofilm formation, and quorum sensing (Kint et al., 2017; Battesti et al., 2015; Bartolini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Inactivation of the GSR promotes the transition to long-term slow growth and antibiotic resistance.
source: Inactivation of the GSR, in turn, promotes the transition to long-term slow growth and antibiotic resistance, which are particularly important for persistent infections (Tuchscherr and Löffler, 2016; Herbert et al., 2010; Bergkessel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Long-term slow growth and antibiotic resistance are particularly important for persistent infections.
source: Inactivation of the GSR, in turn, promotes the transition to long-term slow growth and antibiotic resistance, which are particularly important for persistent infections (Tuchscherr and Löffler, 2016; Herbert et al., 2010; Bergkessel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A member of the PPM family of serine/threonine phosphatases dephosphorylates a phosphorylated substrate protein to activate an alternative σ-factor through a 'partner-switching' mechanism.
source: In a widespread mechanism for initiating the GSR, a member of the PPM family of serine/threonine phosphatases dephosphorylates a phosphorylated substrate protein to activate an alternative σ-factor through a 'partner-switching' mechanism (Hecker et al., 2007), but how the phosphatase receives and is activated by an upstream signal has not been determined.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: How the phosphatase receives and is activated by an upstream signal has not been determined.
source: In a widespread mechanism for initiating the GSR, a member of the PPM family of serine/threonine phosphatases dephosphorylates a phosphorylated substrate protein to activate an alternative σ-factor through a 'partner-switching' mechanism (Hecker et al., 2007), but how the phosphatase receives and is activated by an upstream signal has not been determined.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: RsbU dephosphorylates a single phospho-serine on its substrate protein (RsbV).
source: RsbU dephosphorylates a single phospho-serine on its substrate protein (RsbV) to release the GSR transcription factor (σB) from inhibition by an anti-sigma factor (RsbW; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and referenced in Figure 1A.

claim: Dephosphorylation of RsbV releases the GSR transcription factor (σB) from inhibition by an anti-sigma factor (RsbW).
source: RsbU dephosphorylates a single phospho-serine on its substrate protein (RsbV) to release the GSR transcription factor (σB) from inhibition by an anti-sigma factor (RsbW; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: RsbU has an N-terminal four-helix bundle domain that dimerizes RsbU.
source: RsbU has an N-terminal four-helix bundle domain that dimerizes RsbU and is also the binding site for RsbT, which activates RsbU as a phosphatase (Figure 1C and D; Delumeau et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: The N-terminal four-helix bundle domain of RsbU is the binding site for RsbT.
source: RsbU has an N-terminal four-helix bundle domain that dimerizes RsbU and is also the binding site for RsbT, which activates RsbU as a phosphatase (Figure 1C and D; Delumeau et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: RsbT activates RsbU as a phosphatase.
source: RsbU has an N-terminal four-helix bundle domain that dimerizes RsbU and is also the binding site for RsbT, which activates RsbU as a phosphatase (Figure 1C and D; Delumeau et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and is a foundational statement for the study.

claim: RsbT is sequestered in a megadalton stress sensing complex called the stressosome.
source: RsbT is sequestered in a megadalton stress sensing complex called the stressosome, and is released to bind RsbU in response to specific stress signals including ethanol, heat, acid, salt, and blue light (Hecker et al., 2007; Marles-Wright et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RsbT is released from the stressosome to bind RsbU in response to specific stress signals including ethanol, heat, acid, salt, and blue light.
source: RsbT is sequestered in a megadalton stress sensing complex called the stressosome, and is released to bind RsbU in response to specific stress signals including ethanol, heat, acid, salt, and blue light (Hecker et al., 2007; Marles-Wright et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RsbU activation by RsbT has been reconstituted in vitro.
source: We and others have reconstituted RsbU activation by RsbT (Delumeau et al., 2004; Ho and Bradshaw, 2021), but how RsbT activates RsbU was not known.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research including the authors' previous work.

claim: The mechanism by which RsbT activates RsbU was not known prior to this study.
source: We and others have reconstituted RsbU activation by RsbT (Delumeau et al., 2004; Ho and Bradshaw, 2021), but how RsbT activates RsbU was not known.
evidence: This identifies the knowledge gap addressed by the study.

claim: The amino acid substitution Q94L in RsbU causes enhanced σB activity in B. subtilis.
source: Amino acid substitutions in RsbU (Q94L and M166V) cause enhanced σB activity in B. subtilis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the plate assay shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The amino acid substitution M166V in RsbU causes enhanced σB activity in B. subtilis.
source: Amino acid substitutions in RsbU (Q94L and M166V) cause enhanced σB activity in B. subtilis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the plate assay shown in Figure 1B and was previously reported.

claim: RsbUQ94L activates σB in the absence of rsbT.
source: rsbUQ94L strains activated σB in the absence of rsbT.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B plate assay.

claim: The activation of σB by RsbUQ94L is comparable to when rsbT is overexpressed.
source: This activation is comparable to when rsbT is overexpressed to exceed the capacity of the stressosome and is stronger than what we observe in strains expressing rsbUM166V/L (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B plate assay.

claim: The activation of σB by RsbUQ94L is stronger than what is observed in strains expressing rsbUM166V/L.
source: This activation is comparable to when rsbT is overexpressed to exceed the capacity of the stressosome and is stronger than what we observe in strains expressing rsbUM166V/L (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B plate assay.

claim: In the AlphaFold2 model of RsbU dimer, the linkers form extended alpha-helices (82-112) that cross to connect dimers of the RsbU N-terminal domains and C-terminal phosphatase domains.
source: In our model, the linkers form extended alpha-helices (82-112) that cross to connect dimers of the RsbU N-terminal domains and C-terminal phosphatase domains, with Q94 buried in the linker interface and M166 buried in the core of the phosphatase domain (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on the AlphaFold2 structural prediction shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Q94 is buried in the linker interface in the AlphaFold2 model of RsbU dimer.
source: In our model, the linkers form extended alpha-helices (82-112) that cross to connect dimers of the RsbU N-terminal domains and C-terminal phosphatase domains, with Q94 buried in the linker interface and M166 buried in the core of the phosphatase domain (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on the AlphaFold2 structural prediction shown in Figure 1D.

claim: M166 is buried in the core of the phosphatase domain in the AlphaFold2 model of RsbU dimer.
source: In our model, the linkers form extended alpha-helices (82-112) that cross to connect dimers of the RsbU N-terminal domains and C-terminal phosphatase domains, with Q94 buried in the linker interface and M166 buried in the core of the phosphatase domain (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on the AlphaFold2 structural prediction shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The crossing linker helices in RsbU have similar conformation to homologous linkers observed in crystal structures of Pseudomonas aeruginosa RssB.
source: The crossing linker helices have similar conformation to homologous linkers observed in crystal structures of Pseudomonas aeruginosa RssB, a phosphatase/adapter protein that also controls the GSR (PDB 3F7A and 3EQ2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the AlphaFold2 model with crystal structures.

claim: RssB is a phosphatase/adapter protein that controls the GSR.
source: The crossing linker helices have similar conformation to homologous linkers observed in crystal structures of Pseudomonas aeruginosa RssB, a phosphatase/adapter protein that also controls the GSR (PDB 3F7A and 3EQ2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge.

claim: RssB has an N-terminal response-receiver domain in place of the RsbU four helix bundle dimerization domain.
source: RssB has an N-terminal response-receiver domain in place of the RsbU four helix bundle dimerization domain, suggesting that linker conformation is a conserved feature of PPM phosphatase dimers with divergent N-terminal regulatory domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Linker conformation is a conserved feature of PPM phosphatase dimers with divergent N-terminal regulatory domains.
source: RssB has an N-terminal response-receiver domain in place of the RsbU four helix bundle dimerization domain, suggesting that linker conformation is a conserved feature of PPM phosphatase dimers with divergent N-terminal regulatory domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural similarities.

claim: The linker helices in the RsbU prediction and the RssB structure splay apart as they enter the PPM domain with similar angle.
source: The linker helices in the RsbU prediction and the RssB structure splay apart as they enter the PPM domain with similar angle (pitch angles (α) based on Crick parameters for coiled-coils –17.6° and –18.4°, respectively) and pack against α–1 of the PPM fold (Grigoryan and Degrado, 2011).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Other bacterial signaling proteins that are regulated by coiled-coil linkers have similar pitch angle for the helices connecting to the catalytic domains.
source: Interestingly, we observed that other bacterial signaling proteins that are regulated by coiled-coil linkers had similar pitch angle for the helices connecting to the catalytic domains (for example the dimeric histidine kinase CheA, 1B3Q, α –16.8°, and the dimeric GGDEF diguanylate cyclase PadC, 5LLW, α –14.3°; Bilwes et al., 1999; Gourinchas et al., 2017; Grigoryan and Degrado, 2011; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of multiple proteins.

claim: The linker of RsbU could be a conserved regulatory feature, analogous to linkers of histidine kinases and GGDEF diguanylate cyclases.
source: Thus, the linker of RsbU could be a conserved regulatory feature, analogous to linkers of histidine kinases and GGDEF diguanylate cyclases.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural similarities.

claim: Socket2 analysis identifies amino acids 83–97 of RsbU as a two-turn coiled coil.
source: Analysis of the RsbU dimer model using Socket2 identifies amino acids 83–97 as a two-turn coiled coil, with Q94 unfavorably packing against leucine 90 (Kumar and Woolfson, 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of the structure.

claim: Q94 unfavorably packs against leucine 90 in the RsbU coiled coil.
source: Analysis of the RsbU dimer model using Socket2 identifies amino acids 83–97 as a two-turn coiled coil, with Q94 unfavorably packing against leucine 90 (Kumar and Woolfson, 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of the structure.

claim: Substitutions of Q94 with hydrophobic residues (isoleucine, valine, and methionine) result in mild, RsbT-independent activation of σB.
source: We found that substitutions of Q94 with amino acids that could pack at the intersection of the crossing linker helices (hydrophobic residues isoleucine, valine, and methionine, as well as tyrosine) resulted in mild, RsbT-independent activation of σB that was further heightened by RsbT (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Substitution of Q94 with tyrosine results in mild, RsbT-independent activation of σB.
source: We found that substitutions of Q94 with amino acids that could pack at the intersection of the crossing linker helices (hydrophobic residues isoleucine, valine, and methionine, as well as tyrosine) resulted in mild, RsbT-independent activation of σB that was further heightened by RsbT (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Aromatic hydrophobic residues (phenylalanine and tryptophan) at position 94 drive constitutive activation of RsbU but do not bypass the requirement for rsbT on the chromosome.
source: Aromatic hydrophobic residues (phenylalanine and tryptophan) drove constitutive activation of RsbU but did not bypass the requirement for rsbT on the chromosome (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 (note: the text references the wrong figure supplement).

claim: Substitutions of Q94 with small or charged residues (alanine, glycine, glutamate, and asparagine) do not lead to σB activity.
source: Substitutions of small or charged residues (alanine, glycine, glutamate, and asparagine) did not lead to activity in either strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Burial of the amino acid at position 94 in the crossed helices drives RsbU activation.
source: These results are consistent with a model in which burial of the amino acid at position 94, such as in the crossed helices of our prediction for RsbU dimer structure, drives RsbU activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic data.

claim: RsbT binds to RsbUQ94L with approximately 10-fold higher affinity than to wild-type RsbU.
source: From these data we obtained a KD of 4.5±1 µM, which decreased approximately 10-fold for RsbUQ94L (0.56±0.2 µM; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence anisotropy measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The KD of RsbT binding to wild-type RsbU is 4.5±1 µM.
source: From these data we obtained a KD of 4.5±1 µM, which decreased approximately 10-fold for RsbUQ94L (0.56±0.2 µM; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence anisotropy measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The KD of RsbT binding to RsbUQ94L is 0.56±0.2 µM.
source: From these data we obtained a KD of 4.5±1 µM, which decreased approximately 10-fold for RsbUQ94L (0.56±0.2 µM; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence anisotropy measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RsbUQ94L stimulates RsbU phosphatase activity by an on-pathway mechanism.
source: Thus, RsbUQ94L stimulates RsbU phosphatase activity by an on-pathway mechanism, supporting the idea that RsbT binding stabilizes the linker in a dimerized conformation to activate RsbU.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding affinity data.

claim: RsbT binding stabilizes the linker in a dimerized conformation to activate RsbU.
source: Thus, RsbUQ94L stimulates RsbU phosphatase activity by an on-pathway mechanism, supporting the idea that RsbT binding stabilizes the linker in a dimerized conformation to activate RsbU.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the binding and activity data.

claim: The kcat of wild-type RsbU is 15±0.35 min–1 with RsbT and 1.4±0.077 min–1 without RsbT.
source: The kcat of wild-type RsbU is 15±0.35 min–1 with RsbT and 1.4±0.077 min–1 without RsbT and the kcat of RsbUQ94L is 9.0±0.64 min–1 with RsbT and 2.4±0.084 min–1 without RsbT.
evidence: This is based on phosphatase assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The kcat of RsbUQ94L is 9.0±0.64 min–1 with RsbT and 2.4±0.084 min–1 without RsbT.
source: The kcat of wild-type RsbU is 15±0.35 min–1 with RsbT and 1.4±0.077 min–1 without RsbT and the kcat of RsbUQ94L is 9.0±0.64 min–1 with RsbT and 2.4±0.084 min–1 without RsbT.
evidence: This is based on phosphatase assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The KMMnCl2 of wild-type RsbU is 0.98±0.069 mM with RsbT and 77±9.0 mM without RsbT.
source: The KMMnCl2 of wild-type RsbU is 0.98±0.069 mM with RsbT and 77±9.0 mM without RsbT and the KMMnCl2 of RsbUQ94L is 1.4±0.19 mM with RsbT and 1.9±0.56 mM without RsbT.
evidence: This is based on phosphatase assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The KMMnCl2 of RsbUQ94L is 1.4±0.19 mM with RsbT and 1.9±0.56 mM without RsbT.
source: The KMMnCl2 of wild-type RsbU is 0.98±0.069 mM with RsbT and 77±9.0 mM without RsbT and the KMMnCl2 of RsbUQ94L is 1.4±0.19 mM with RsbT and 1.9±0.56 mM without RsbT.
evidence: This is based on phosphatase assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: RsbUQ94L has a KM for MnCl2 that is more than 50-fold reduced compared to RsbU alone.
source: However, RsbUQ94L had a KM for MnCl2 (1.4±0.2 mM) that is more than 50-fold reduced compared to RsbU alone (77±9 mM; Ho and Bradshaw, 2021), and similar to the KMMnCl2 of RsbU in the presence of RsbT (0.98±0.07 mM Ho and Bradshaw, 2021; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on phosphatase assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The KM for MnCl2 of RsbUQ94L is similar to the KMMnCl2 of RsbU in the presence of RsbT.
source: However, RsbUQ94L had a KM for MnCl2 (1.4±0.2 mM) that is more than 50-fold reduced compared to RsbU alone (77±9 mM; Ho and Bradshaw, 2021), and similar to the KMMnCl2 of RsbU in the presence of RsbT (0.98±0.07 mM Ho and Bradshaw, 2021; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on phosphatase assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Addition of RsbT does not change the KM of RsbUQ94L for MnCl2.
source: Addition of RsbT did not change the KM of RsbUQ94L for MnCl2 (1.9±0.6 mM), but the maximum catalytic rate of dephosphorylation increased nearly four-fold to 9.0±0.64 min–1, approaching the rate of RsbU stimulated by RsbT (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on phosphatase assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Addition of RsbT increases the maximum catalytic rate of dephosphorylation by RsbUQ94L nearly four-fold.
source: Addition of RsbT did not change the KM of RsbUQ94L for MnCl2 (1.9±0.6 mM), but the maximum catalytic rate of dephosphorylation increased nearly four-fold to 9.0±0.64 min–1, approaching the rate of RsbU stimulated by RsbT (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on phosphatase assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: RsbUQ94L substantially recapitulates RsbT activation by decreasing the KM for Mn2+.
source: Thus, RsbUQ94L substantially recapitulates RsbT activation by decreasing the KM for Mn2+, demonstrating that the linker transduces RsbT binding to control the active site of RsbU (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic data.

claim: The linker transduces RsbT binding to control the active site of RsbU.
source: Thus, RsbUQ94L substantially recapitulates RsbT activation by decreasing the KM for Mn2+, demonstrating that the linker transduces RsbT binding to control the active site of RsbU (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic data.

claim: The allosteric switch controlling phosphatase activity of SpoIIE couples dimerization to cofactor interaction.
source: This is consistent with previous findings that the allosteric switch controlling phosphatase activity of SpoIIE couples dimerization to cofactor interaction.
evidence: This is supported by prior research on SpoIIE.

claim: In the AlphaFold2 prediction of the 2RsbT/2RsbU complex, RsbU adopts a conformation very similar to the prediction of the RsbU dimer.
source: In this model, RsbU adopts a conformation very similar to our prediction of the RsbU dimer (RMSD 1.36 Å), suggesting that our AlphaFold2 RsbU dimer model represents the active state of RsbU even when RsbT was not included in the prediction (a known feature of AlphaFold2 models Chakravarty and Porter, 2022).
evidence: This is based on comparison of AlphaFold2 models.

claim: The AlphaFold2 RsbU dimer model represents the active state of RsbU.
source: In this model, RsbU adopts a conformation very similar to our prediction of the RsbU dimer (RMSD 1.36 Å), suggesting that our AlphaFold2 RsbU dimer model represents the active state of RsbU even when RsbT was not included in the prediction (a known feature of AlphaFold2 models Chakravarty and Porter, 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural similarity and cited knowledge about AlphaFold2.

claim: The predicted structure places RsbT in a hybrid interface that spans the N-terminal dimerization domain of both RsbU monomers and the linker of one monomer.
source: The predicted structure places RsbT in a hybrid interface that spans the N-terminal dimerization domain of both RsbU monomers and the linker of one monomer (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on the AlphaFold2 prediction shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Residues previously implicated in RsbT/U binding (Y28 and E24 from one RsbU monomer, I74, and I78 from the other RsbU monomer, and RsbT R19, R23, and N24) are all buried in the predicted interface.
source: Supporting the validity of the AlphaFold2 2RsbT/2RsbU model, residues previously implicated in RsbT/U binding (Hardwick et al., 2007; Y28 and E24 from one RsbU monomer, I74, and I78 from the other RsbU monomer, and RsbT R19, R23, and N24) are all buried in the predicted interface (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the AlphaFold2 prediction and prior genetic data.

claim: A genetic screen isolated 11 variants that introduced substitutions to RsbU that suppress rsbUY28I: S49G, K53E, T89A, G92E, G92R, Q94L, T110S, V142A, K143E, C165Y, and M173I.
source: After screening a library of PCR mutagenized rsbUY28I and rsbT, we identified 11 variants that introduced substitutions to RsbU that suppress rsbUY28I: S49G, K53E, T89A, G92E, G92R, Q94L, T110S, V142A, K143E, C165Y, and M173I (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is based on a genetic screen shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Revertants that restored Y28 were isolated in the genetic screen, suggesting that the screen was near saturation.
source: We additionally isolated revertants that restored Y28 suggesting that the screen was near saturation, but did not isolate any suppressors in rsbT, which was also mutagenized.
evidence: This is based on the genetic screen results.

claim: No suppressors in rsbT were isolated in the genetic screen.
source: We additionally isolated revertants that restored Y28 suggesting that the screen was near saturation, but did not isolate any suppressors in rsbT, which was also mutagenized.
evidence: This is based on the genetic screen results.

claim: RsbUY28I suppressor mutations fall into three classes: substitutions in the RsbU N-terminal dimerization domain near the predicted RsbT binding site, substitutions near predicted contacts between RsbT and the RsbU linker, and substitutions that cluster around the regulatory switch element of the RsbU phosphatase domain.
source: Mapping the RsbUY28I suppressor mutations onto our 2RsbU/2RsbT model suggests that they fall into three classes (Figure 3A and B): (1) Substitutions in the RsbU N-terminal dimerization domain that map near the predicted RsbT binding site (S49G and K53E), supporting the predicted interface. (2) Substitutions that map near predicted contacts between RsbT and the RsbU linker (T89A, G92E/R, and Q94L), providing evidence that contacts between RsbT and the linker promote RsbU activation. (3) Substitutions that cluster around the regulatory switch element of the RsbU phosphatase domain (helices α1 and α2 of the PPM fold, T110S, V142A, K143E, C165Y, and M173I).
evidence: This is based on mapping the mutations onto the AlphaFold2 model.

claim: Substitutions in the RsbU N-terminal dimerization domain that map near the predicted RsbT binding site (S49G and K53E) support the predicted interface.
source: Mapping the RsbUY28I suppressor mutations onto our 2RsbU/2RsbT model suggests that they fall into three classes (Figure 3A and B): (1) Substitutions in the RsbU N-terminal dimerization domain that map near the predicted RsbT binding site (S49G and K53E), supporting the predicted interface.
evidence: This is based on mapping the mutations onto the AlphaFold2 model.

claim: Substitutions that map near predicted contacts between RsbT and the RsbU linker (T89A, G92E/R, and Q94L) provide evidence that contacts between RsbT and the linker promote RsbU activation.
source: (2) Substitutions that map near predicted contacts between RsbT and the RsbU linker (T89A, G92E/R, and Q94L), providing evidence that contacts between RsbT and the linker promote RsbU activation.
evidence: This is based on mapping the mutations onto the AlphaFold2 model.

claim: Substitutions that cluster around the regulatory switch element of the RsbU phosphatase domain (T110S, V142A, K143E, C165Y, and M173I) rescue RsbUY28I inactivation by reducing the energetic cost to transition the RsbU phosphatase domain to the active conformation.
source: (3) Substitutions that cluster around the regulatory switch element of the RsbU phosphatase domain (helices α1 and α2 of the PPM fold, T110S, V142A, K143E, C165Y, and M173I). We hypothesize that these substitutions rescue RsbUY28I inactivation by reducing the energetic cost (normally provided by RsbT binding) to transition the RsbU phosphatase domain to the active conformation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the location of the mutations.

claim: The genetic data provide independent support for the AlphaFold2 model of the 2RsbT/2RsbU complex.
source: Together these genetic data provide independent support for the AlphaFold2 model of the 2RsbT/2RsbU complex, and suggest that RsbT activates RsbU by transmitting signals to the switch element in the RsbU phosphatase domain through a coiled-coil linker.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic data.

claim: RsbT activates RsbU by transmitting signals to the switch element in the RsbU phosphatase domain through a coiled-coil linker.
source: Together these genetic data provide independent support for the AlphaFold2 model of the 2RsbT/2RsbU complex, and suggest that RsbT activates RsbU by transmitting signals to the switch element in the RsbU phosphatase domain through a coiled-coil linker.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic and structural data.

claim: RsbUR91E abolished σB activity for cells overexpressing rsbT.
source: RsbUR91E abolished σB activity for cells overexpressing rsbT (Figure 3C), and in biochemical assays RsbT stimulation of RsbUR91E phosphatase activity was abolished (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on genetic and biochemical assays shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: RsbT stimulation of RsbUR91E phosphatase activity was abolished.
source: RsbUR91E abolished σB activity for cells overexpressing rsbT (Figure 3C), and in biochemical assays RsbT stimulation of RsbUR91E phosphatase activity was abolished (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on biochemical assays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Expression of rsbTD92K partially restored σB activity to rsbUR91E expressing cells.
source: Finally, we introduced a potentially compensatory charge switch at position D92 of RsbT (RsbTD92K; Figure 3C). Expression of rsbTD92K partially restored σB activity to rsbUR91E expressing cells, consistent with direct interaction between these residues (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on genetic assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The partial restoration of σB activity by rsbTD92K to rsbUR91E expressing cells is consistent with direct interaction between R91 of RsbU and D92 of RsbT.
source: Expression of rsbTD92K partially restored σB activity to rsbUR91E expressing cells, consistent with direct interaction between these residues (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic data.

claim: Contacts between RsbT and the linker of RsbU are responsible for phosphatase activation.
source: Together, these results suggest that contacts between RsbT and the linker of RsbU are responsible for phosphatase activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic and biochemical data.

claim: RsbU eluted as a single peak from the size exclusion column with an average molecular weight of 77 kDa determined by multi-angle light scattering.
source: RsbU eluted as a single peak from the size exclusion column with an average molecular weight of 77 kDa (calculated dimeric molecular weight 77.3 kDa) determined by multi-angle light scattering (MALS; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The calculated dimeric molecular weight of RsbU is 77.3 kDa.
source: RsbU eluted as a single peak from the size exclusion column with an average molecular weight of 77 kDa (calculated dimeric molecular weight 77.3 kDa) determined by multi-angle light scattering (MALS; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a calculated value based on the protein sequence.

claim: The RsbU sample had a minor contaminant of heterodimeric complexes of RsbU in which one monomer is C-terminally truncated.
source: However, our sample had a minor contaminant of heterodimeric complexes of RsbU in which one monomer is C-terminally truncated that could influence the SAXS analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on SDS-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: EFA deconvolution identified a major component with MW 75.6 kDa and a smaller component with MW 48.8 kDa.
source: The EFA deconvolution identified a major component (MW 75.6 kDa calculated from Vc method), which eluted earlier than a smaller component (MW 48.8 kDa calculated from Vc method; Table 1 Guinier fits, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Table 1.

claim: The larger component from EFA deconvolution is a RsbU dimer.
source: We conclude that the larger component is a RsbU dimer, while the smaller fragment is likely a heterodimeric complex of RsbU and the C-terminal truncation product of RsbU (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular weight and gel analysis.

claim: The smaller component from EFA deconvolution is likely a heterodimeric complex of RsbU and the C-terminal truncation product of RsbU.
source: We conclude that the larger component is a RsbU dimer, while the smaller fragment is likely a heterodimeric complex of RsbU and the C-terminal truncation product of RsbU (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular weight and gel analysis.

claim: The scattering intensity profile of RsbU was a poor fit (χ2 12.53) to a profile calculated from the AlphaFold2 model of an RsbU dimer using FoXS.
source: Indicative of significant deviation between the RsbU structure in solution to the AlphaFold2 model, the scattering intensity profile (I(q) vs. q) was a poor fit (χ2 12.53) to a profile calculated from the AlphaFold2 model of an RsbU dimer using FoXS (Schneidman-Duhovny et al., 2016; Schneidman-Duhovny et al., 2013; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The scattering intensity data for RsbU lacked distinct features caused by the multi-domain structure of RsbU from the AlphaFold2 model.
source: First, the scattering intensity data lacked distinct features caused by the multi-domain structure of RsbU from the AlphaFold2 model (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The dimensionless Kratky plot for RsbU is bell-shaped and peaks above 1.3, indicating that the RsbU dimer is non-globular.
source: This can be visualized more readily from a dimensionless Kratky plot, which is bell-shaped and peaks above 1.3, indicating that the RsbU dimer is non-globular (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The P(r) plot for RsbU is smooth and has an extended tail, indicating flexibility.
source: The scattering data had several additional characteristic features indicating flexibility: the P(r) plot is smooth and has an extended tail (Cordeiro et al., 2017; Kikhney and Svergun, 2015; Receveur-Brechot and Durand, 2012; Figure 4C)
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Rg and I(0) calculated from P(r) for RsbU are larger than when calculated from Guinier fits, indicating flexibility.
source: Rg and I(0) calculated from P(r) are larger than when calculated from Guinier fits (Cordeiro et al., 2017; Kikhney and Svergun, 2015; Receveur-Brechot and Durand, 2012; Table 1)
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Molecular weight calculated using the MoW2 modified Porod volume method for RsbU is an overestimate, indicating flexibility.
source: molecular weight calculated using the MoW2 modified Porod volume method is an overestimate (Rambo and Tainer, 2011; Table 1)
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The Rg of RsbU (39.05±0.16 Å) was larger than the Rg of the AlphaFold2 dimer model (34.05 Å).
source: and the Rg (39.05±0.16 Å) was larger than the Rg of the AlphaFold2 dimer model (34.05 Å).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis.

claim: MultiFoXS produced a two-state solution with χ2 of 1.2 for RsbU.
source: MultiFoXS produced a two-state solution with χ2 of 1.2 (as compared to the one-state model with χ2 of 12.5) and low residuals across the entire range of data (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The one-state model for RsbU had a χ2 of 12.5.
source: MultiFoXS produced a two-state solution with χ2 of 1.2 (as compared to the one-state model with χ2 of 12.5) and low residuals across the entire range of data (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis.

claim: Flexibility was allowed for linker residues 82–96 in the MultiFoXS analysis while keeping the N-terminal domain dimerized.
source: We allowed flexibility for the linker residues 82–96 while keeping the N-terminal domain dimerized because a stable dimer of the N-terminal domain is observed in solution, was present in a previous X-ray crystal structure of C-terminally truncated RsbU{Delumeau:2004ep}, and C-terminally truncated RsbU coelutes as a heterodimer with the full-length protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on prior structural data and the current SEC data.

claim: The precise region of allowed linker flexibility does not have a substantial impact on the MultiFoXS fit.
source: Importantly, the precise region of allowed linker flexibility does not have a substantial impact on the MultiFoXS fit (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), but constraining the C-terminal phosphatase domain dimer does not yield a good fit to the data (χ2 of 5.4; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Constraining the C-terminal phosphatase domain dimer does not yield a good fit to the SAXS data (χ2 of 5.4).
source: Importantly, the precise region of allowed linker flexibility does not have a substantial impact on the MultiFoXS fit (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), but constraining the C-terminal phosphatase domain dimer does not yield a good fit to the data (χ2 of 5.4; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The structural models predicted by MultiFoXS depict a dimerized N-terminal domain with flexible linkers and PPM domains that do not make contact.
source: The structural models predicted by MultiFoXS depict a dimerized N-terminal domain with flexible linkers and PPM domains that do not make contact.
evidence: This is based on the MultiFoXS analysis.

claim: The two conformations selected as the best fit to the scattering data by MultiFoXS have very different Rg values (34.91 Å [71%] and 45.69 Å [29%]).
source: The two conformations that were selected as the best fit to the scattering data by MultiFoXS also have very different Rg values, (34.91 Å [71%] and 45.69 Å [29%]), indicating RsbU samples a range of conformational space that includes a more compact state(s) consistent with the AlphaFold2 model and a significantly extended state(s), emphasizing that the linker is highly flexible.
evidence: This is based on the MultiFoXS analysis.

claim: RsbU samples a range of conformational space that includes a more compact state consistent with the AlphaFold2 model and a significantly extended state.
source: The two conformations that were selected as the best fit to the scattering data by MultiFoXS also have very different Rg values, (34.91 Å [71%] and 45.69 Å [29%]), indicating RsbU samples a range of conformational space that includes a more compact state(s) consistent with the AlphaFold2 model and a significantly extended state(s), emphasizing that the linker is highly flexible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MultiFoXS analysis.

claim: The RsbU linker is highly flexible in the absence of RsbT.
source: Together, we conclude that the RsbU linker appears to be flexible in the absence of RsbT (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the SAXS data analysis.

claim: The RsbT/UQ94L complex eluted with an average molecular weight of 125 kDa determined by MALS.
source: The RsbT/UQ94L complex eluted as a major peak with a higher molecular weight shoulder (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 4; also visible when we ran RsbUQ94L alone. Figure 4—figure supplement 1), with the average molecular weight of the main peak (determined by MALS) of 125 kDa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The predicted molecular weight of a heterotetrameric 2RsbT/2RsbUQ94L complex is 105 kDa.
source: This is larger than the predicted molecular weight of a heterotetrameric 2RsbT/2RsbUQ94L complex (105 kDa), suggesting that some higher order complexes form.
evidence: This is a calculated value based on the protein sequences.

claim: Some higher order complexes of RsbT/UQ94L form.
source: This is larger than the predicted molecular weight of a heterotetrameric 2RsbT/2RsbUQ94L complex (105 kDa), suggesting that some higher order complexes form.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MALS molecular weight.

claim: EFA deconvolution of RsbT/UQ94L identified a component with SAXS molecular weight of 164 kDa and a component with SAXS molecular weight of 103 kDa.
source: EFA deconvolution (Meisburger et al., 2016) identifies two components. The first deconvolved component had a SAXS determined molecular weight of 164 kDa, while the second had a SAXS molecular weight of 103 kDa, consistent with a 2RsbT/2RsbU complex (105 kDa).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis.

claim: The second component from EFA deconvolution of RsbT/UQ94L is a 2RsbT/2RsbU hetero-tetramer.
source: Together with the fact that RsbT co-elutes with RsbUQ94L throughout the entire peak (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and the MALS molecular weight, we assess that this second component is an 2RsbT/2RsbU hetero-tetramer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular weight and co-elution data.

claim: The Rg from the Guinier fit for the 2RsbT/2RsbUQ94L complex (35.06±0.43 Å) matches well with the model computed from the AlphaFold2 prediction (33.68 Å).
source: First, the Rg from the Guiner fit (35.06±0.43 Å) matches well with the model computed from the AlphaFold2 prediction of the heterotetrameric complex of 2RsbT/2RsbU using FoXS (33.68 Å) and is smaller than the Rg we observed for the RsbU dimer (39.05±0.16 Å).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis.

claim: The Rg of the 2RsbT/2RsbUQ94L complex is smaller than the Rg observed for the RsbU dimer.
source: First, the Rg from the Guiner fit (35.06±0.43 Å) matches well with the model computed from the AlphaFold2 prediction of the heterotetrameric complex of 2RsbT/2RsbU using FoXS (33.68 Å) and is smaller than the Rg we observed for the RsbU dimer (39.05±0.16 Å).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis.

claim: The features of the scattering data suggest that the RsbT/RsbU complex is more rigid than RsbU dimers.
source: Second, the features of the scattering data that suggested flexibility for RsbU dimers all suggest that the RsbT/RsbU complex is more rigid (the quality of the FoXS fit, a lower peak of the dimensionless Kratky plot, and a shorter tail of the P(r) plot; Cordeiro et al., 2017; Kikhney and Svergun, 2015; Receveur-Brechot and Durand, 2012; Figure 4C, E, F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis shown in Figures 4C, E, F.

claim: Fitting the scattering profile of the 2RsbT/2RsbUQ94L complex to the AlphaFold2 model yielded a χ2 of 1.83 without requirement for flexibility.
source: Third, fitting the scattering profile (I(q) vs. q) to the AlphaFold2 model yielded a χ2 of 1.83 without requirement for flexibility (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The AlphaFold2 model of the heterotetrameric 2RsbT/2RsbU complex is valid.
source: Together, these data support the validity of the AlphaFold2 model of the heterotetrameric 2RsbT/2RsbU complex, and additionally suggest that RsbT rigidifies the otherwise flexible linker of RsbU to dimerize the phosphatase domains (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the SAXS data analysis.

claim: RsbT rigidifies the otherwise flexible linker of RsbU to dimerize the phosphatase domains.
source: Together, these data support the validity of the AlphaFold2 model of the heterotetrameric 2RsbT/2RsbU complex, and additionally suggest that RsbT rigidifies the otherwise flexible linker of RsbU to dimerize the phosphatase domains (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the SAXS data and biochemical data.

claim: B. subtilis has a second GSR-initiating PPM phosphatase, RsbP, that has an N-terminal PAS domain.
source: B. subtilis has a second GSR-initiating PPM phosphatase, RsbP, that has an N-terminal PAS domain and dephosphorylates RsbV to activate σB in response to energy stress.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge.

claim: RsbP dephosphorylates RsbV to activate σB in response to energy stress.
source: B. subtilis has a second GSR-initiating PPM phosphatase, RsbP, that has an N-terminal PAS domain and dephosphorylates RsbV to activate σB in response to energy stress.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge.

claim: The AlphaFold2 prediction of an RsbP dimer shows an extended alpha-helical linker connecting dimeric PAS domains and phosphatase domains.
source: Our AlphaFold2 prediction of an RsbP dimer shows an extended alpha-helical linker connecting dimeric PAS domains and phosphatase domains.
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold2 structural prediction.

claim: The interface between the dimerized phosphatase domains of RsbP is predicted to be mediated by α1 and α2 of the phosphatase domain.
source: Like RsbU, the interface between the dimerized phosphatase domains is predicted to be mediated by α1 and α2 of the phosphatase domain.
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold2 structural prediction.

claim: Previously identified constitutively activating mutations in RsbP map to similar positions as the gain-of-function mutations identified for RsbU.
source: We found that previously identified constitutively activating mutations in RsbP (Brody et al., 2009) map to similar positions as the gain-of-function mutations we identified here for RsbU in their respective predicted structures, namely the interface between α1 and α2 of the phosphatase domains and the linker.
evidence: This is based on mapping mutations onto AlphaFold2 predictions.

claim: RsbP is activated by a partner-protein, RsbQ, that has analogous function to RsbT for RsbU.
source: RsbP is activated by a partner-protein, RsbQ, that has analogous function to RsbT for RsbU.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge.

claim: An AlphaFold2 prediction of the heterotetrameric 2RsbP/2RsbQ complex places the two molecules of RsbQ in a hybrid interface between the PAS domains and linkers, similar to how RsbT contacts RsbU.
source: An AlphaFold2 prediction of the heterotetrameric 2RsbP/2RsbQ complex places the two molecules of RsbQ in a hybrid interface between the PAS domains and linkers, similar to how RsbT contacts RsbU.
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold2 structural prediction.

claim: RsbP is controlled through an activation mechanism similar to that of RsbU.
source: These predictions suggest a testable hypothesis that RsbP is controlled through an activation mechanism similar to that of RsbU (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural predictions.

claim: AlphaFold2 produced high-confidence predictions of phosphatase domains dimerized through a shared α0, α1, α2 interface for diverse GSR initiating phosphatases.
source: In each case, AlphaFold2 produced high-confidence predictions of phosphatase domains dimerized through a shared α0, α1, α2 interface, connected to dimeric N-terminal domains by crossing α-helical linkers (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold2 structural predictions.

claim: The AlphaFold2 models for many of the predicted phosphatase structures have unfavorable polar residues buried in the coiled-coil interface.
source: Consistent with a model in which the stability of the linker plays a conserved regulatory role, the AlphaFold2 models for many of the predicted structures have unfavorable polar residues buried in the coiled-coil interface (positions a and d, for which non-polar residues are most favorable; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of AlphaFold2 predictions shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Linker-mediated phosphatase domain dimerization is an evolutionarily conserved, adaptable mechanism to control PPM phosphatase activity.
source: From this analysis, we speculate that linker-mediated phosphatase domain dimerization is an evolutionarily conserved, adaptable mechanism to control PPM phosphatase activity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural analysis.

claim: σB was the first conditionally activated cellular transcription factor to be identified, discovered 45 years ago.
source: Since the ground-breaking discovery of σB, the first conditionally activated cellular transcription factor to be identified, 45 years ago (Haldenwang and Losick, 1979), a persistent unanswered question has been how σB is turned on.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original discovery.

claim: RsbT activates RsbU by rigidifying an otherwise flexible linker region to allosterically activate RsbU as a phosphatase.
source: Using unbiased genetic screens, biochemical reconstitution, biophysical approaches, and structural prediction, we have discovered that RsbT activates RsbU by rigidifying an otherwise flexible linker region to allosterically activate RsbU as a phosphatase.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by multiple lines of evidence.

claim: RsbU linkers assume a crossed α-helical conformation that dimerizes the phosphatase domains.
source: Our structural prediction, supported by our genetic and structural data suggest that RsbU linkers assume a crossed α-helical conformation that dimerizes the phosphatase domains (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by structural predictions and SAXS data.

claim: Dimerization of RsbU phosphatase domains activates RsbU through a conserved switch element at the dimer interface, decreasing the KM for metal cofactor and increasing the catalytic rate.
source: This dimerization activates RsbU through a conserved switch element at the dimer interface, decreasing the KM for metal cofactor and increasing the catalytic rate.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical data.

claim: The mechanism of linker-mediated phosphatase domain dimerization is a widespread mechanism to regulate the activity of bacterial protein serine/threonine phosphatases.
source: Our structural predictions suggest that this is a widespread mechanism to regulate the activity of bacterial protein serine/threonine phosphatases.
evidence: This is an inference based on AlphaFold2 predictions of multiple phosphatases.

claim: E. coli RssB and B. subtilis RsbU use three shared regulatory features to control GSR activation: positioning of analogous flexible linkers, the interface between the linker and α1 of the phosphatase domain, and conformational change of the switch helices.
source: Our findings reveal that E. coli RssB and B. subtilis RsbU use three shared regulatory features to control GSR activation through their distinct downstream mechanisms. First, the positioning of analogous flexible linkers controls GSR activation by RssB and RsbU (Brugger et al., 2023a; Brugger et al., 2023b; Dorich et al., 2019). ... Second, the interface between the linker and α1 of the phosphatase domain is critical for regulation of both RssB and RsbU (Brugger et al., 2023a; Dorich et al., 2019). ... Third, conformational change of the switch helices (α1 and α2) of the phosphatase domain is of shared regulatory importance (Battesti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with prior research on RssB.

claim: The C-terminal pseudo-phosphatase domain of RssB is joined to its N-terminal σS binding response-receiver domain by a predominantly α-helical linker of similar length to the linker of RsbU.
source: The C-terminal pseudo-phosphatase domain of RssB is joined to its N-terminal σS binding response-receiver domain by a predominantly α-helical linker (termed the segmented helical linker, or SHL) of similar length to the linker of RsbU (Dorich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The SHL of RssB folds to occlude the σS interacting face of the response-receiver domain when bound to anti-adapters.
source: The SHL folds to occlude the σS interacting face of the response-receiver domain when bound to anti-adapters, and is remodeled to promote σS interaction when the response-receiver domain is phosphorylated (Brugger et al., 2023a; Brugger et al., 2023b; Dorich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Substitution of W143 in RssB, the homologous residue to Q94 of B. subtilis RsbU, blocks regulation by IraD and IraP.
source: Supporting the hypothesis that the SHL is mechanistically related to the RsbU linker, substitution of W143, the homologous residue to Q94 of B. subtilis RsbU, blocks regulation by IraD and IraP (Battesti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: W143 of RssB packs in a hydrophobic pocket formed with the α1 helix of the pseudo-phosphatase domain of phosphorylated RssB and IraD-bound RssB.
source: W143 packs in a hydrophobic pocket formed with the α1 helix of the pseudo-phosphatase domain of phosphorylated RssB and IraD-bound RssB (Brugger et al., 2023a; Dorich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Substitution of residues in α1 of RssB, including A216 (corresponding to M166 of RsbU), block regulation of RssB by anti-adapters.
source: Substitution of residues in α1, including A216 (corresponding to M166 of RsbU), block regulation of RssB by anti-adapters, underscoring the mechanistic similarity (Battesti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: HDX experiments demonstrate that there is decreased exchange of the α1 helix of the pseudo-phosphatase domain of RssB when σS is bound.
source: HDX experiments demonstrate that there is decreased exchange of the α1 helix of the pseudo-phosphatase domain of RssB when σS is bound, suggesting that the conformational dynamics of this region are reduced by substrate recognition (Brugger et al., 2023a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Key regulatory features were conserved when an ancestral phosphatase lost enzymatic activity and became a dedicated adapter protein in E. coli and related γ-proteobacteria.
source: These striking mechanistic similarities between RssB from E. coli and RsbU from B. subtilis suggest that key regulatory features were conserved when an ancestral phosphatase lost enzymatic activity and became a dedicated adapter protein in E. coli and related γ-proteobacteria.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanistic similarities.

claim: P. aeruginosa has a homologue of RssB/RsbU that functions as an adapter for σS degradation and has a catalytically active, full-length phosphatase domain.
source: Interestingly, P. aeruginosa has a homologue of RssB/RsbU that functions as an adapter for σS degradation, yet has a catalytically active, full-length phosphatase domain and resides in an operon with an rsbV homologue (rssC; Rodríguez-Martínez et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Crystal structures of P. aeruginosa RssB revealed that it forms a dimer with crossing linkers and dimerized phosphatase domains with striking similarity to the dimer predicted for RsbU.
source: Crystal structures of P. aeruginosa RssB revealed that it forms a dimer with crossing linkers and dimerized phosphatase domains with striking similarity to the dimer predicted for RsbU (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of crystal structures with AlphaFold2 predictions.

claim: Adapter protein function of P. aeruginosa RssB requires RssC.
source: Intriguingly, adapter protein function of P. aeruginosa RssB requires RssC (Rodríguez-Martínez et al., 2023), and E. coli RssB has been observed to weakly dimerize (Dorich et al., 2019), further supporting a direct mechanistic link between phosphatase regulation and adapter protein function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: E. coli RssB has been observed to weakly dimerize.
source: Intriguingly, adapter protein function of P. aeruginosa RssB requires RssC (Rodríguez-Martínez et al., 2023), and E. coli RssB has been observed to weakly dimerize (Dorich et al., 2019), further supporting a direct mechanistic link between phosphatase regulation and adapter protein function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Linker-mediated control of a PPM phosphatase is a broadly conserved mechanism for GSR initiation across bacterial phyla.
source: While not all GSR regulatory mechanisms involve a phosphatase or adapter protein related to RsbU/RssB, these findings suggest that linker-mediated control of a PPM phosphatase is a broadly conserved mechanism for GSR initiation across bacterial phyla.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative analysis.

claim: Histidine kinases and GGDEF diguanylate cyclases are often active in dimeric complexes that are allosterically controlled by N-terminal regulatory domains that propagate signals through crossing α-helical linkers.
source: A striking feature of their regulatory mechanisms is that they are often active in dimeric complexes that are allosterically controlled by N-terminal regulatory domains that propagate signals through crossing α-helical linkers (Zschiedrich et al., 2016; Randall et al., 2022; Gourinchas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The crossing α-helical linkers of RsbU are structurally similar to those of histidine kinases and GGDEF diguanylate cyclases.
source: Our findings that the crossing α-helical linkers are structurally similar (Fig. S2C) and that shared regulatory domains (response receiver, HAMP, and PAS domains) connect phosphatase dimers by a coiled-coil linker (Figure 5A-C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) suggests that this shared allosteric regulatory architecture allows modular exchange of N-terminal domains between PPM phosphatases, histidine kinases, and GGDEF diguanylate cyclases (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: Shared regulatory domains (response receiver, HAMP, and PAS domains) connect phosphatase dimers by a coiled-coil linker.
